source.title: Network Dissection: Quantifying Interpretability of Deep Visual Representations
source.authors: David Bau; Bo-Lei Zhou; A. Khosla; A. Oliva; A. Torralba

record.tranche_reason: The study measures how individual CNN units align with labeled visual concepts, not whether representations from different models align. It reports that different random initializations reach similar interpretability levels and relates this to convergent learning, but does not measure shared features, subspaces, or representational similarity.
record.gate_note: The study compares semantic interpretability scores, including across architectures, tasks, training conditions, and random initializations. Those scores do not measure model-to-model alignment or shared features. The reported random-initialization result is recorded under fits_no_version as a related but different construct. Other interpretability results, including the basis-rotation experiment, are not rows because they do not measure the claim’s convergence outcomes.
record.test_reason: Network Dissection scores how well single units align with Broden concepts in each CNN. It never compares one model's representations, features or units with another's, so its results do not bear on any convergence version. The random-initialization result (Sec. 3.5, Fig. 11) compares only aggregate detector counts across seeds. The authors link it to convergent learning [16] in a single sentence, which is discussion rather than a test.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that interpretability is axis-aligned and not implied by discriminative power: random rotations cut unique detectors by 80% at equal accuracy. They also find it depends on architecture, supervision, layer and training conditions such as batch normalization. Their only convergence-related remark is that random initializations converge to similar interpretability levels, consistent with [16].
record.recipe_differences: Uses unit-to-concept alignment against Broden labels and intersection-over-union scores, rather than measuring convergence or representational similarity between models.
record.method_sensitivity: Interpretability varies with training task, architecture, layer, and training conditions; these are not sensitivity tests of a model-to-model similarity measure.

fits_no_version.finding: Three randomly initialized Places205-AlexNet repeats reach similar levels of interpretability, in both unique-detector and total-detector counts, at about 50.0% top-1 accuracy each.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different random seeds yield similar aggregate unit-interpretability levels. This does not establish that they learn the same features.

fits_no_version.finding: Units detecting the same Broden concepts (e.g. house, dog, train, airplane) appear in ResNet-152, GoogLeNet and VGG-16, all trained on Places365. Their counts and IoUs differ across architectures (Fig. 6, Fig. 7).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Detectors for the same human-labelled concepts emerge in different CNN architectures. Their number depends on architecture and training task, and their correspondence across models is unmeasured.

record.problems: The result relevant to random initializations concerns aggregate interpretability counts, not feature identity or representational alignment. The reported comparison is qualitative in the text and its plotted values are not given numerically. Interpretability scores also depend on the concepts represented in Broden, whose coverage the authors note is incomplete.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows: the paper's architecture, task, layer, rotation, and training-condition results measure unit interpretability, not the model-to-model alignment or shared features specified by the claim.

untested.parts: No model-to-model alignment measure, so nothing on whether alignment rises with scale or capability. Depth and width are related only to interpretability.
No language models and no image–caption pairs.
Seeds are compared only on detector counts. The study does not check which units or concepts match across seeds, nor any shared subspace.
No mapping, stitching or relative representations between models. The rotation experiment is within one model.
Detectors for the same Broden concepts are labelled in several architectures (Fig. 6). The study does not test whether these are corresponding or equivalent features across models.
No cross-model similarity measure whose settings or inputs could be varied.
No measure of how complete or plateaued alignment is, and no test of its causes.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification is upheld. This is not an original source. The cross-architecture concept detectors in Fig. 6 are the closest content to V5, but they are per-model labels rather than a test of feature recurrence or equivalence, so they are recorded under fits_no_version rather than as a row.

versions.untested_parts: Does not measure whether alignment between independently trained models rises with model size or capability.
Does not compare vision and language models or paired images and captions.
Compares interpretability levels across random initializations, but does not test whether the models learn the same features or shared subspaces.
Does not test mappings, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
Identifies semantic detectors in several models but does not test recurrence or equivalence of the same features or circuits across models.
Does not vary similarity measures, their settings, or inputs for a model-to-model convergence measure.
Does not measure whether model-to-model alignment plateaus or whether shared training data or objectives explain it.

relation.reason: Figure 6 reports the study's own comparison of detectors for the same concepts across three architectures, bearing on V5. The claim that it never compares features or units across models overlooks this result.

tranche.reason: Section 3.4 and Figure 6 compare recurring semantic detectors across ResNet-152, GoogLeNet and VGG-16 trained on Places365. These unit-to-concept measurements bear on V5 through a different method, although the recorded aggregate seed comparisons do not establish V3.

source_check.notes: Missing V5 evidence: Figure 6 compares house, dog, train, plant and airplane detectors across three architectures. Similar detector counts across seeds alone do not establish shared features or subspaces.
